facts.text: The yellow-rumped thornbill is the largest thornbill, at 9.5–12 cm long and weighing about 9 grams.
facts.quote: The yellow-rumped thornbill is the largest species of thornbill, 9.5–12 cm (3.7–4.7 in) long and weighing 9 g (0.32 oz).

facts.text: It has a distinctive yellow rump, a black forehead with white spots, a grey head and neck, and a white line above the eye.
facts.quote: The species has a distinctive yellow rump, a black forehead with white spots, grey head and neck, a white line above the eye and white throat.

facts.text: Its song is described as twittering, musical, sweet and high-pitched, and it mimics other birds, especially the alarm calls of the noisy miner.
facts.quote: The yellow-rumped thornbill has a distinctive song described as "twittering, musical, sweet, high-pitched". The species is also reported to be an accomplished mimic of other birds, in particular mimicking the alarm calls of the noisy miner.

facts.text: It mainly eats ants, beetles, bugs and lerps, and usually forages in small groups of 3 to 12 birds.
facts.quote: major prey items include ants, beetles, bugs and lerps. Other items eaten include spiders, flies and seeds. The species usually forages in small groups of between 3 and 12 individuals

facts.text: Its dome-shaped nest has a false cup-shaped nest on top, while the real nest inside has a concealed entrance.
facts.quote: Atop the dome is a cup-shaped depression which serves as a false nest, while the real nest is inside with a concealed entrance.

facts.text: Breeding runs from July to December, with one, two or more broods a year, and one to three helpers sometimes assist the breeding pair.
facts.quote: Breeding takes place from July to December, with one, two or even more broods a year. Nesting usually occurs as a pair, but sometimes one to three helpers will assist the breeding pair.

facts.text: The female incubates the three or four dull-white eggs, which take around 16 to 18 days to hatch.
facts.quote: A clutch of three or four dull-white oval eggs, lightly spotted with red-brown mostly at the large end and each measuring 18 mm × 13 mm (0.71 in × 0.51 in), is laid. The female incubates the clutch, and the clutch takes around 16–18 days to hatch.

facts.text: Both the shining bronze-cuckoo and the fan-tailed cuckoo parasitise its nests.
facts.quote: The species is parasitised by the shining bronze-cuckoo and the fan-tailed cuckoo.

facts.text: Ringing studies show the species can live for up to nine years.
facts.quote: Ringing studies have found that the species can live for up to nine years.

facts.text: Australian birdwatchers affectionately call it the butterbum.
facts.quote: Butterbum is a colloquial name used by Australian birdwatchers.
